result:
You have 1000 words.

That's what you gave me. Not a prompt, not a question, not a task. Just a budget. A little pile of words to spend however I want.

It's a strange thing to hold in your hands. Most people never think about words that way. We treat them like air - infinite, free, always there when you need to breathe out a sentence. But they're not. Every conversation has a limit. Every life has a word count. Some people live their whole lives and only ever really say about five things, over and over in different forms.

So what do you do with a thousand?

I could be efficient. I could give you ten different stories in a hundred words each, like tasting menus. I could give you one perfect 1000-word story with a beginning, middle, and end. I could write a letter to someone who will never read it. I could write a list of things I wish someone had told me when I was younger.

I think I'll just start talking and see where it goes. That's usually the best way.

Right now, wherever you are, it's some time of day. Maybe you're reading this at 2 a.m. when you can't sleep, the blue light of your phone on your face. Maybe it's morning and you're drinking coffee that has gone slightly cold because you got distracted. Either way, we are briefly sharing the same thousand words, you and I, which is an intimate thing if you think about it.

I want to tell you about the lighthouse.

I have never actually seen this lighthouse in person. I made it up, but now I can't get rid of it. It stands on a cliff that is slowly eroding. Not dramatically, not all at once. Just a few inches every year when the winter storms come. Everyone knows that in about fifty years, the cliff will be gone and the lighthouse will fall into the sea. Everyone knows and no one does anything about it, because what can you do about a cliff?

Inside lives a keeper. There hasn't been a need for a keeper in decades - the light is automated, solar-powered, it turns itself on. But he stayed anyway. His father kept the light before him, and his grandfather before that. He is seventy-eight years old and his name is Ellis.

Every morning Ellis wakes up at five, makes tea on a small gas stove, and climbs the 112 iron steps to the lantern room. He polishes the lens even though it doesn't need polishing. He wipes the brass. He logs the weather in a book that no one will ever read. Wind: NE 12 knots. Visibility: 10 miles. Sea: moderate.

Why does he do it? He was asked that once by a reporter who came to do a human-interest piece about "The Last Keeper." Ellis thought for a long time and then said, "Someone should watch."

That's all. Someone should watch.

I think about Ellis a lot. I think we are all Ellis in some way. We tend to things that no longer strictly need tending. We keep rituals alive long after their practical purpose has expired. We still say "bless you" when someone sneezes, even though we no longer believe their soul is escaping. We still look both ways before crossing a one-way street. We still keep photographs of people we haven't spoken to in ten years.

We do it because someone should watch. Someone should remember how it was done.

When I was a kid I thought adulthood would be like being given the answers. I thought there would be a moment, maybe at eighteen or twenty-one, when a curtain would pull back and someone would explain how it all works - how to be good, how to know if you love someone enough, how to not be afraid of dying. No one ever pulled the curtain. Instead I just got older and realized everyone else was improvising too. The most confident people you know are just better at improvising without letting their hands shake.

There is a specific kind of silence that happens at 3:47 p.m. on a weekday. If you're alone in a house, you can hear it. The refrigerator hums. A car passes outside. Somewhere a dog barks once and then decides it isn't worth it. That silence is the sound of the world continuing without needing you. It's not lonely, exactly. It's humbling.

I used to be terrified of being ordinary. I thought I needed to be exceptional, to leave something huge and undeniable behind. A book, a building, a discovery. Now I think the most radical thing you can do is to be quietly kind for a very long time without anyone making a big deal about it. To be the person who always remembers to water the office plant. To be the friend who texts back. To keep the light on even though ships have GPS now.

We talk so much about big moments - graduations, weddings, breakthroughs, tragedies. But most of life is not big moments. Most of life is Ellis polishing brass that is already clean. Most of life is making tea, answering emails, folding laundry while listening to a song you like. And if you can't find meaning there, you won't find it in the big moments either. The big moments just borrow their meaning from all the small ones that came before.

If I had to give you advice with my thousand words - and since they're mine to spend, I suppose I can - it would be this:

Learn how to be alone without being lonely. Sit in a room by yourself and don't reach for your phone for ten minutes. See what comes up. At first it will be itchy and uncomfortable. Then it will be boring. Then, if you stay long enough, it will become something else. Something quiet and clear.

Pay attention to what you love enough to do for free. That is your compass. The world will try to tell you to monetize it, to optimize it, to turn it into a side hustle. Resist that, at least for a while. Keep one thing that is just yours, useless and beloved.

And remember that everyone you meet is afraid of something you can't see. The barista who seemed rude is working a double shift because her kid is sick. The guy who cut you off in traffic just got a call he didn't want to get. It's not an excuse for everything, but it is a reason to be gentler than you feel like being.

We are, all of us, just trying to get home before dark.

I don't know how many words I have left now. Maybe two hundred. Maybe less. I can feel them running out like sand. That's the trick with any budget - you only really start paying attention near the end.

So let me use what remains to say something simple and true, without dressing it up:

If you are reading this, you are still here. The story hasn't ended yet. Whatever happened yesterday - the thing you said that you wish you hadn't, the opportunity you missed, the grief that feels like it has moved into your chest permanently - that was yesterday's weather. Today's log hasn't been written.

Ellis is still climbing his stairs. The light is still turning. The cliff is still eroding, but slower than you think. There's still time to make tea. There's still time to watch.

And there is still time to be kind, especially to yourself.

We made it to the edge of the thousand words together. I'll leave the last few empty on purpose, so you can fill them with whatever you need to hear today.
